why: A subarray l..r-1 is flagged when (S[r] - S[l]) mod k == r - l. Since a remainder is always < k, its length must be < k, and then the condition is (S[r] - r) mod k == (S[l] - l) mod k. That is the 'count equal prefix keys with a hash map' pattern, restricted to a sliding window of the last k-1 prefixes.
hints: Write the subarray sum as a difference of prefix sums S[r] - S[l] and its length as r - l.
A remainder is between 0 and k-1, so only subarrays of length < k can qualify. For those, move everything to one side: key(i) = (S[i] - i) mod k must match.
Scan r = 0..n with a counter of keys for prefix indices in [r-k+1, r-1]: add counter[key(r)] to the answer, insert key(r), and remove key(r-k+1) when it falls out. O(n) time.
pitfalls: Forgetting the length < k restriction overcounts: a subarray of length k has key equality but remainder 0, not k.
Include the empty prefix S[0] = 0 at index 0.
The count can reach about n^2/2, so use a 64-bit result.
statement:
You are given an array pid of n positive integers and an integer k. A contiguous subarray is malicious when

(sum of the subarray) mod k == length of the subarray

Return the number of malicious subarrays (subarrays at different positions count separately).

Example: pid = [1, 3, 2, 4], k = 4.

  • [1]: sum 1, 1 mod 4 = 1, length 1. Malicious.
  • [3]: 3 mod 4 = 3, length 1. No. [2]: 2 vs 1. No. [4]: 0 vs 1. No.
  • [1,3]: 4 mod 4 = 0 vs 2. No. [3,2]: 5 mod 4 = 1 vs 2. No. [2,4]: 6 mod 4 = 2, length 2. Malicious.
  • [1,3,2]: 6 mod 4 = 2 vs 3. No. [3,2,4]: 9 mod 4 = 1 vs 3. No. [1,3,2,4]: 10 mod 4 = 2 vs 4. No.

The answer is 2.
